extracted.intended_audience: web writers, UX/content designers, and anyone creating online text
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing short, scannable, and well-structured web pages that use hypertext effectively so readers can quickly find and consume information. Emphasizes brevity, layered headings, emphasis, accessibility, and hypertext organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct
rubrics_metrics.description: write no more than 50% of the text you would have used in a hardcopy publication
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading from screens is about 25% slower than paper and users feel unpleasant reading online; therefore write roughly 50% less text (not just 25% less). Keep pages short to reduce scrolling and user displeasure. Rationale/evidence: user studies and screen-readability differences (screen dpi constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for scannability
rubrics_metrics.description: don't require users to read long continuous blocks of text; users scan text and pick out keywords, sentences, and paragraphs of interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume users skim rather than read full streams of text. Make key information easy to spot so skimmers can find what they need. This behavior is confirmed by numerous usability studies; write to match scanning patterns rather than linear reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypertext to split up long information into multiple pages
rubrics_metrics.description: split the information up into multiple nodes connected by hypertext links so each page can be brief yet the full hyperspace contains more content than a printed article
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put long/detailed background on secondary pages and provide links for minority-interest information so readers who don't want it aren't penalized. Avoid sacrificing depth: use linked pages to preserve detail while keeping primary pages short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use hypertext to segment a long, linear story into multiple pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypertext should not be used to segment a long, linear story (e.g., 'continued on page 2')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segmenting linear narratives into multiple downloads slows reading and complicates printing. Proper hypertext breaks content into coherent, topical chunks rather than forced sequential pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertext structure should be based on audience analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: build the link structure so readers can select topics they care about and only download those pages
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the site’s information architecture around audience needs and topic-based selection; this allows personalization of download/reading effort and prevents forcing all readers to fetch irrelevant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each hypertext page should use the inverse-pyramid principle and start with a short conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: start with a short conclusion so users can get the gist even if they don't read the whole page
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write each page so the most important information appears first; detailed background follows. This supports skimming and lets readers judge relevance at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure articles with 2–3 levels of headlines (nested headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: use a general page heading plus subheads — and sub-subheads when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nested headings break text for skimmers, make sections discoverable, and facilitate navigation. They also help accessibility (screenreaders) by providing semantic structure for blind users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meaningful rather than cute headings
rubrics_metrics.description: reading a heading should tell the user what the page or section is about
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clever or vague headings; clear, descriptive headings let scanners and screenreader users know what content follows and improve findability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use highlighting and emphasis to make important words stand out
rubrics_metrics.description: use highlighting, emphasis, colored text, and links so important words catch the user's eye
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic emphasis sparingly to signal key terms and sentences. Colored text can emphasize; hypertext anchors naturally stand out (blue, underlined). Ensure emphasis aids scanning rather than creating visual clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep pages short to avoid excessive scrolling
rubrics_metrics.description: users dislike scrolling, so pages should be kept short
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short pages reduce scrolling friction and increase perceived readability. Combine with hypertext chunking to maintain depth without long single pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split information into coherent topical chunks
rubrics_metrics.description: split information into coherent chunks that each focus on a certain topic
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each chunk/page should be a self-contained topic so readers can select topics of interest independently; coherence improves comprehension and prevents fragmented reading experiences.
